newsitem.title: PERU: Peru iron miner Shougang says investments on track.
newsitem.headline: Peru iron miner Shougang says investments on track.

text.p: Chinese-owned iron miner Shougang Hierro Peru, which struggled with a lack of investment in its first years following privatization, says it has overcome early problems and is confident of fulfilling new commitments.

"We have committed ourselves to invest $137 million in Peru which we will be able to carry out, since we have taken care to find a better reception for our products," Shougang President Wong Jin Rui said in an interview.
He said the company has focused since last year on improving mineral processing, especially pellets due to their higher demand compared with Shougang's sinter output.
The firm's sinter contains one percent of sulphur impurities while Asian clients do not accept any more than 0.3 percent and therefore prefer Australian and Brazilian producers, he added.

Peru's only iron producer, Shougang formally pledged last year to invest $137 million up to 2000, principally to construct a new production line that would double output of pellets to six million tonnes per year.
Under a timetable worked out with Peru's privatization board, Shougang was to invest $10 million in 1996, $27 million in 1997 and $100 million the following two years.

Shougang Corp, China's state iron company, bought Peru's state-run Hierro Peru S.A. and its facilities at Marcona, 250 miles south of Lima, in November 1992 for $120 million and a commitment to invest $150 million over three years.
Despite that initial commitment, the company only invested $34.8 million in the period, drawing protests from officials and leading to the new investment timetable.
Shougang's general manager, Raul Vera La Torre, said the firm invested $12.6 million in 1996, with $4 million of that used for a prospecting program.

"We need reserves for 20 or 30 years to assure the pellet production. We believe that we have this after the studies were carried out. That is fundamental information for an investment program of this type," said Vera La Torre.
He added that Shougang was also interested in building a coal-fired power station at a cost of $300 million to support its expansion plans.
"The feasibility studies are ready," he said. "The power station would be ready in 1999, which would open the possibility of expanding operations in the following years."
Shougang's principal clients include local companies Sider Peru, with an annual demand of 630,000 tonnes and Aceros Arequipa, which accounts for 100,000 tonnes per year.
The company's total productin fell 27.2 percent last year to 2.8 million tonnes, largely due to labor disputes.

In January 1997, iron production continued falling by 17.2 percent to 257,851 tonnes versus the same month last year. But the company is confident of reverting the trend in the second quarter, officials said.
